papers.title: Beyond Greenwashing: Algorithmic Resilience and the Non-Linear Governance Premium in Sovereign Capital Flows
papers.abstract: Despite the proliferation of sovereign Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) metrics, traditional linear macro-financial models systematically misprice Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) tail risks during systemic shocks. This paper demonstrates that sovereign risk transmission is fundamentally non-linear. Using a forward-chained global panel of 147 sovereign entities (2010-2024), we deploy a gradient boosting architecture that compresses forecast errors by over 39% against L1-regularized baselines precisely during extreme macroeconomic tail events. Moving beyond opaque predictive accuracy, we apply dual interpretability frameworks to mathematically map the discrete threshold effects of institutional quality. We identify a strict, non-linear "Governance Premium": incremental environmental and social improvements yield zero capital advantage until a foundational regulatory threshold is breached. Finally, we establish regime-conditional 95% uncertainty bounds that maintain valid marginal coverage even under severe ESG reporting failures. This framework equips policymakers with a distribution-free tool to quantify sovereign tail-risk, proving that global capital markets price institutional resilience as a discrete boundary rather than a continuous premium.

papers.title: Testing strong exogeneity in proxy SVARs with internal synthetic proxies
papers.abstract: Proxy SVARs often rely on a single credible proxy, leaving proxy exogeneity untestable. Narrative arguments used to justify proxy validity imply a stronger form of exogeneity. We formalize the strong exogeneity assumption and propose a corresponding test based on internal synthetic proxies. The approach uses the external proxy to locate the target-shock direction in the reduced-form innovations and synthesize the candidate shock into an additional internal synthetic proxies, which allows to test the joint exogeneity of the original and internal synthetic proxy. We derive the large-sample theory for the ISP test and show that the identification strength is governed by a direct measure of the target shock's non-Gaussianity. We study weak identification under asymptotic Gaussianity and develop an identification-robust version of the test. Monte Carlo experiments demonstrate the favorable power of the test when the proxy has a low signal-to-noise ratio. Applications to monetary policy and oil supply news shocks find no evidence against the exogeneity of the benchmark proxies.

papers.title: Indirect inference in incomplete and partially identified econometric models
papers.abstract: We extend the indirect inference principle to structural econometric models that are incomplete, in the sense that a single value of the structural parameter may be compatible with multiple distributions of the observed endogenous variables, so that the structural parameter is typically only partially identified. We define the binding function as the smallest norm of the auxiliary estimating equations over the set of data generating processes compatible with the structural model. Hence, we obtain a confidence region by inverting a test of the hypothesis that the binding function vanishes at the pseudo-true value. A dual characterization based on random set theory makes the binding function computationally tractable. We define the auxiliary model conditionally on the covariates to remove its dependence on the unknown covariate distribution and we show that the binding function is Lipschitz and Hadamard directionally differentiable, so that the numerical delta method delivers valid critical values. We show that the method provides significant computational advantages without relinquishing informativeness in a simulation experiment based on an entry game with 100 potential entrants.

papers.title: Many Hands Make Light Work: Long-Term Effect Inference for the Experiment Reservoir
papers.abstract: The surrogate index method is the modern standard for estimation of long-term effects in a designed experiment using only short-term outcomes. This method relies on the surrogacy and comparability assumptions which may be violated in practice leading to estimation bias. We propose a new method called Experiment Reservoir Surrogate (ERS) which leverages a reservoir of historical long-term experiments that is common in large-scale experimentation platforms. ERS avoids the surrogacy assumption by predicting the long-term average treatment effect directly, and relaxes the comparability assumption by matching to similar historical experiments, without requiring every experiment in the reservoir to be comparable to the target experiment. Moreover, ERS is memory-efficient, as it only requires aggregate data for each time period, instead of raw individual-level data. We theoretically justify the improved efficiency of ERS and demonstrate the improvement empirically on a reservoir of experiments from the online platform DoorDash.

papers.title: Bias Correction and Inference for Panel Quantile Regression
papers.abstract: We develop a large-$n$, large-$T$ theory for the unsmoothed fixed-effects quantile regression estimator, paralleling Hahn and Newey (2004) for smooth nonlinear panel models. An exact rank-score identity for the profiled criterion, with a convexity argument, delivers the leading incidental parameter bias of the slope estimator, of order $T^{-1}$, in closed form. When $n$ and $T$ grow at the same rate, the estimator is asymptotically normal but in general not centred, and conventional intervals are invalid. Admissible growth of $n$ relative to $T$, up to $n=o(T^3)$, depends on the regularity of the conditional error densities. A split-panel jackknife removes the leading bias throughout this range and yields valid inference. In serially dependent panels whose dependence decays geometrically or polynomially, the bias acquires a term from the dependence between regressors and errors of different periods, the jackknife remains valid with contiguous but not with interleaved half-panels, and clustered standard errors are valid.

papers.title: Time-Varying Quantile VAR Models: Estimation and Inference
papers.abstract: We study time-varying quantile VAR models in which the conditional quantile does not propagate linearly through the recursion, and develop a toolkit for impulse response analysis, which to the best of our knowledge has not been established elsewhere. For example, we establish Bahadur representation for quantile VAR regression, infer model parameters via smoothed check function, and define and investigate the best linear projection of the time-varying tau-quantile impulse response via local projections. An application to U.S. industrial production growth and credit spreads from 1919-2025 uncovers structural shifts in tail relationships, demonstrating downside asymmetry diminishes at longer forecast horizons.

papers.title: A Semiparametric Real-Time GARCH Model with Nonstationary Variance
papers.abstract: We propose a semiparametric real-time GARCH (SRT-GARCH) model that combines a smooth deterministic long-run volatility component with a stationary short-run process driven by contemporaneous return innovations. The model accommodates gradual changes in unconditional variance while allowing short-run volatility to respond directly to current information rather than relying solely on lagged observations. We derive the variance normalization, conditional moments, and closed-form conditional density of the model. For estimation, we develop a two-step procedure that combines kernel smoothing with conditional Gaussian maximum likelihood. Under Gaussian innovations and mild regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the short-run parameter estimator. The analysis exploits geometric moment contraction to control serial dependence and shows that estimating the long-run component adds a positive semidefinite rank-one adjustment to the oracle covariance matrix obtained when the long-run component is known. The resulting asymptotic covariance matrix admits a plug-in estimator that requires neither lag truncation nor additional tuning parameters. Monte Carlo simulations show good finite-sample performance of the estimator and the associated inference procedure. Applications to FTSE~100 returns and U.S. natural gas futures show that allowing for a time-varying long-run component improves forecasting relative to the parametric RT-GARCH benchmark, while the additional real-time feedback mechanism provides more pronounced gains in the natural gas application than in the FTSE application. The proposed model also delivers competitive one-step-ahead Value-at-Risk forecasts.

papers.title: Identifying and disentangling direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
papers.abstract: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. We show that both components are identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, without an uncontaminated comparison group. Under no anticipation, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for covariates by machine learning, and establish asymptotic normality. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.

papers.title: Personal preference or system role? Battery swapping among UK electric vehicle users
papers.abstract: Battery swapping replaces a depleted EV battery with a charged one, reducing waiting time and enabling off-peak charging. Evidence on acceptance, however, remains concentrated in Asian markets, and most studies examine individual adoption intentions. This study asks whether current UK EV users judge swapping differently as a purchase option and as a technology for the transport system. Using Behavioural Reasoning Theory, an integrated choice and latent variable model, and latent class analysis, we analyse perceived usefulness, energy-system concerns, practical barriers, and satisfaction with current charging. Usefulness and energy-system concerns relate more strongly to expectations about the system. Battery compatibility and station coverage relate more strongly to personal preference, while spare battery costs relate to expectations about network viability. User groups differ in how they balance benefits, barriers, and satisfaction with existing charging. Policy should address driver barriers and network viability as distinct but connected priorities.

papers.title: Probabilistic Causal Panel Analysis
papers.abstract: Many causal panel estimators construct counterfactuals using weights or latent structure estimated directly from observed outcomes, making treatment-effect estimates sensitive to observation noise. Bayesian hierarchical models can account for this noise and borrow information across related observations, but existing Bayesian approaches to causal panel analysis generally combine outcome modeling and counterfactual imputation in estimator-specific formulations that can require bespoke sampling algorithms. We develop a framework that learns the latent untreated panel with a probabilistic model and applies established causal estimators to its posterior draws. The model accommodates non-Gaussian observations and structured pooling, while re-estimation across draws propagates uncertainty through counterfactual imputation. We establish conditions for posterior consistency of counterfactual imputation, characterize how pooling affects imputation risk, and develop fast cross-validation for model selection and calibration of predictive uncertainty for treatment effects. Our results show that probabilistic modeling can improve counterfactual imputation, particularly when observation noise is substantial and the pooling structure is informative.

papers.title: Contemporaneous Transmission Networks and Systemic Risk in European Banking
papers.abstract: We study how contemporaneous equity-return transmission shapes systemic exposure among 51 listed European banks. Using a recursive non-Gaussian network model on volatility-standardized returns, we construct two market-capitalization-weighted measures based on direct and indirect transmission effects: the Systemic Impact Score (SIS), capturing a bank's potential influence on other institutions, and the Systemic Vulnerability Score (SVS), capturing its exposure to disturbances originating elsewhere. The fitted network reveals distinct transmitting and receiving roles, highlighting differences between institutions with substantial outward influence and those with high incoming sensitivity. Receiving roles are generally more reproducible than transmitting roles across repeated network discovery, and selected connections remain informative about lower-tail dependence in subsequent observations. Volatility standardization substantially reduces detected dependence among recovered shocks, although the full-sample model does not satisfy the designated criterion for supporting shock independence. Alternative recursive orderings also yield comparable directional tail asymmetries, limiting the extent to which these patterns validate a particular ordering. The results provide complementary measures of model-implied systemic transmission and vulnerability, with explicit attention to uncertainty and identification limits

papers.title: Demand Estimation with Unobserved Stockout Substitution: Exact Likelihood Maximization
papers.abstract: When a product is sold out, customers who prefer it may buy a substitute or leave without purchasing. Efficient demand estimation in this setting is challenging when inventory is observed only at replenishments, because the stockout times, and hence the products available to each customer, are unobserved. Estimating demand efficiently under stockout substitution has been a challenging problem since Anupindi et al. (1998), and it has become more pressing as the scale of such problem instances grows thanks to innovations in retailing such as unmanned stores. We provide a complete solution to this problem for the multinomial logit (MNL) model, the most widely used model of customer choice. Using a continuous-time representation of the purchase process developed in Zhou et al. (2026), we show that the exact likelihood and its gradient are one-dimensional integrals, no matter how many products, customers, or stockouts there are. Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.

papers.title: A Balanced Parametrization of Correlation Matrices
papers.abstract: We introduce the balanced correlation parametrization (BCP), which maps positive-definite correlation matrices one-to-one onto the set of symmetric hollow (zero-diagonal) matrices with unrestricted off-diagonal entries. A key feature of the parametrization is that both the transformation and its inverse are available in closed form. It can be viewed as a generalization of the transformation underlying the classical correlation $t$-statistic to higher dimensions. It has a direct interpretation as a scaled sum of marginal and partial correlations, is inverse-consistent and equivariant under variable permutations and sign changes, and preserves block structure. A novel property of BCP is that it preserves correlation sparsity as the dimension tends to infinity under suitable factor conditions, providing a basis for sparse high-dimensional correlation modeling. An empirical illustration using standardized idiosyncratic daily stock returns for 1,765 equities over 15 years shows that BCP retains the approximate sparsity pattern and magnitudes of shock correlations, and that it yields accurate positive-definite reconstructions under sparse coordinate restrictions.

papers.title: Efficient estimation of structural VARs with higher-order moments
papers.abstract: This paper provides a practical standard for efficient implementation of GMM estimation of structural vector autoregressions identified via higher-order moments. We establish conditions under which the structural estimator is adaptive to reduced-form estimation and the conventional weighting is asymptotically optimal. Despite this optimality, its feasible implementation can be unstable because the covariance of the moments involves many higher-order co-moments. We propose exploiting the same identifying assumption for a structured, bias-corrected covariance estimation under both mutual independence and the weaker mean independence, which also allows for common volatility. The resulting estimator is both asymptotically and computationally efficient. Monte Carlo experiments show substantial gains over conventional GMM and performance comparable to likelihood-based estimators under independent shocks. Under common volatility, the mean-independence estimator remains close to the truth while competing estimators are biased. An oil-market application illustrates the practical gains of the approach.

papers.title: Sharp Testable Implications of Encouragement Designs
papers.abstract: This paper studies a potential outcome model with a continuous or discrete outcome, a discrete multi-valued treatment, and a discrete multi-valued instrument. We derive sharp, closed-form testable implications for a class of restrictions on potential treatments where each value of the instrument encourages towards at most one unique treatment choice; such restrictions serve as the key identifying assumption in several prominent recent empirical papers. Borrowing the terminology used in randomized experiments, we call such a setting an encouragement design. The testable implications are inequalities in terms of the conditional distributions of choices and the outcome given the instrument. Through a novel constructive argument, we show these inequalities are sharp in the sense that any distribution of the observed data that satisfies these inequalities is compatible with this class of restrictions on potential treatments. Based on these inequalities, we propose tests of the restrictions. In an empirical application, we show some of these restrictions are violated and pinpoint the substitution pattern that leads to the violation.

papers.title: Valid Post-Contextual Bandit Inference
papers.abstract: Contextual multi-armed bandits (CMAB) are increasingly used as adaptively sampled experiments, after which researchers test hypotheses about treatment effects. We derive the H\'ajek-Le Cam limit experiment for multi-armed contextual bandits under equal-arms (weak-signal) asymptotics. It is Locally Asymptotically Quadratic, but not a (mixed) Gaussian shift experiment. Girsanov's theorem gives it a structural representation in stochastic differential equations. Together with a general weak convergence result, this yields the asymptotic null distribution and local asymptotic power of often-used test statistics. Two kinds of nuisance parameters threaten size control: the common reward level of the arms of interest and the rewards of the arms not of interest. The first threat is removed by translation-invariant sampling. We propose Regularized Translation-Invariant (RTI) versions of Thompson, tempered-greedy, tempered-(Lin)UCB, and exploration sampling. The second threat calls for appropriate pivots. The structural representation of the limit experiment is key to overcome the inferential challenges arising from adaptive sampling. Simulations corroborate the theory.

papers.title: Cohort-Anchored HonestDiD
papers.abstract: HonestDiD sensitivity analysis (Rambachan and Roth, 2023) is usually applied to event-study coefficients aggregated across cohorts. Under staggered adoption, the treated cohorts contributing to these coefficients change with event time, as do their control groups with estimators that use not-yet-treated units. Therefore, the restriction on the aggregated coefficients and the corresponding inference does not have a clear interpretation. This paper proposes to do the HonestDiD sensitivity analysis on a cohort basis. The restriction is placed on each cohort's block bias, which captures its violation of parallel trends relative to the units untreated when it first adopts treatment. The restriction on the block bias maps to the restriction on the estimation bias through an invertible linear decomposition. In simulations, the proposed cohort inference keeps nominal coverage when parallel trend violations differ across cohorts, where the inference based on aggregated coefficients can fail. Applying the method to Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) and Bailey and Goodman-Bacon (2015), I highlight the trade-off between interpretable imposed restrictions and the precision demands of cohort inference.

papers.title: Transmission channels, dynamic mediation, and higher-order impulse responses
papers.abstract: Impulse responses measure the total effect of causal changes (or shocks) but do not show how that effect is divided among mediator variables. We use the recursion between Sims and higher-order impulse responses (Dufour and Renault, 1998) to decompose an impulse response into the contributions of mediator variables at every propagation stage. A mediator's contribution is the product of an exposure margin, which measures how the shock moves the mediator, and a propagation margin, the multi-horizon projection coefficients that carry these movements over to the outcome. We show that multi-horizon Granger noncausality from a mediator to the outcome implies a zero propagation margin and that a mediator's contribution equals a controlled mediator-path effect. We provide inference for the contributions and a test of the propagation margin. Applying the decomposition to U.S. oil supply news shocks, we find that consumer-price movements in the first six months make a large contribution to the subsequent decline in industrial production, whereas the contribution of the federal funds rate is small throughout.

papers.title: Evaluating A/B Testing Methodologies via Sample Splitting: Theory and Practice
papers.abstract: We develop a theoretical framework for sample splitting in A/B testing environments, where data for each test are partitioned into two splits to measure methodological performance when the true impacts of tests are unobserved. We show that sample-split estimators are generally biased for full-sample performance but consistently estimate sample-split analogues of it. We derive their asymptotic distributions, construct valid confidence intervals, and characterize the bias-variance trade-offs underlying sample-split design choices. We validate our theoretical results through simulations and provide implementation guidance for A/B testing products seeking to evaluate new estimators and decision rules.

papers.title: Distribution-Matching Posterior Inference for Incomplete Structural Models
papers.abstract: Distribution-matching posterior inference (DMPI) extends the minimal econometric interpretation to generalized posterior inference and model comparison for incomplete structural models. It combines a structural-parameter prior with exact Dirichlet-multinomial scores comparing empirical and model-implied distributions of selected population moments. Ensemble size controls structural discipline, and annealed sequential Monte Carlo computes posterior and generalized evidence. In New Keynesian Phillips Curve simulations, a stochastically singular model remains useful under moderate discipline despite failing as an exact representation. In a U.S. three-equation New Keynesian DSGE application, restoring full rank raises or lowers generalized evidence depending on the structural innovation added.

papers.title: On the Use of Design-Based Simulations
papers.abstract: Design-based simulations hold outcomes fixed and generate variation by resampling treatment assignment or shocks. They can be used in both methodological and applied work to assess inference procedures. However, their informativeness for these uses is not straightforward. We show that, when treatment effects are nonzero, these simulations can be misleading about spatial or serial correlation in clustered experiments, difference-in-differences, and shift-share designs. We analyze alternatives and formalize how these simulations can reveal features of the error distribution despite holding outcomes fixed. Finally, we consider limitations in the use of design-based simulations to select among different inference methods in applied work.

papers.title: Nonlinear Drivers of Macroeconomic Tail Risk: A Threshold Stochastic Volatility-in-Mean VAR with Regime-Dependent Leverage
papers.abstract: The tails of macroeconomic outcomes can respond differently from the centre of their distribution to aggregate shocks. We demonstrate this via a threshold stochastic-volatility-in-mean VAR with regime-dependent leverage. The model allows interactions between the endogenous variables and their volatility, contemporaneous level-volatility dependence, and regime-specific propagation. We estimate the model using a long-run U.S. data set, finding evidence for three inflation-based regimes. We identify business-cycle, financial, macroeconomic-uncertainty, and financial-uncertainty shocks and decompose their contributions to growth- and inflation-at-risk. Business-cycle shocks dominate the median response of GNP growth but account for a substantially smaller share of growth-at-risk. In contrast, uncertainty makes a material contribution to both growth- and inflation-at-risk.
